title: Your Penthouse Sells Itself. Why Your One-Bedroom Units Do Not
seoTitle: Your Penthouse Sells Itself. Your One-Bedrooms Do Not
description: Most presale launch budgets go to the penthouse. Why the one-bedroom buyer needs more to look at, and why you should spend where the doubt is.
answer: In a presale, the penthouse almost always sells. The hard units are the one-bedrooms on the lower floors. Most launch budgets go to renderings of the top floors, leaving the sales team with hundreds of smaller units and nothing to show. The one-bedroom buyer has less money and more fear, so spend where the doubt is and show small units with the same care.
body:
Your penthouse will sell. It always does. The problem in most presale launches is not the top of the building. It is the one-bedroom on the fourth floor.

## Where most launch budgets go

Look at a typical launch. The visual budget goes to the units that sell themselves. Ten beautiful renderings of the top floors. The terrace, the skyline view, the big living room at sunset.

Then the launch is over and the sales team faces reality. They have 200 smaller units to move and nothing to show for them. The material that exists was made for the units that never needed help.

## The one-bedroom buyer has more fear

Think about who buys each unit.

- **The penthouse buyer** usually has more money and more room for risk. The product is rare, and it is easy to want.
- **The one-bedroom buyer** has less money and more fear. For many of them, this is a stretch, maybe their first purchase off-plan. Every dollar matters, and every unknown feels bigger.

And what do we give the more nervous buyer? Less to look at. A generic floorplan, maybe a shared amenity image, and a lot of imagination. That is the opposite of what they need.

## Spend where the doubt is

The rule I use is simple: spend where the doubt is. The units with the most doubt deserve the most clarity, not the least.

In practice, that means:

1. Show the small units with the same care as the penthouse.
2. Give the lower-floor buyer the same quality of visuals the top-floor buyer gets.
3. Make sure the sales team has something to show for every unit they need to sell, not just the best ones.

## Why this changes your sales pace

The smaller units are usually the bulk of the building. That is where your sales slow down when buyers cannot picture what they are paying for. It is also where your sales can speed up, once those buyers can see their unit as clearly as the penthouse buyer sees theirs.

The penthouse will take care of itself. Your attention, and your budget, belong with the one-bedroom on the fourth floor.
takeaways: The penthouse almost always sells; the smaller units are the real challenge.
Most launch budgets go to renderings of the top floors.
The one-bedroom buyer has less money and more fear, yet gets less to look at.
Spend where the doubt is and show small units with the same care as the penthouse.
Smaller units are where presale sales slow down, and where they can speed up.
faq: Why do one-bedroom presale units sell slower than penthouses?
Their buyers usually have less money and more fear, and they often get less visual material to understand what they are buying. More doubt with less information slows the decision.
How should a developer split the presale marketing budget?
Spend where the doubt is. Instead of putting most of the visuals into the top floors, make sure the smaller units that make up most of the building are shown with the same care.
Do penthouse renderings help sell the rest of the building?
They can build desire for the project, but they do not answer the questions of a buyer looking at a one-bedroom on a lower floor. That buyer needs to see their own unit.
